payload.detail: full build and test suite green

findings.suggestion: Make the constraint and the query agree: either add `CREATE INDEX ix_customers_upper_email ON customers (upper(email))`, or change the finder to an explicit JPQL `where lower(c.email) = lower(:email)` so the lower(email) index serves both roles. Confirm before shipping by turning on `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.show_sql` in a test run to capture the generated predicate, then EXPLAIN it against a customers table seeded with ~100k rows and check for Index Scan rather than Seq Scan.
findings.summary: The new unique index is on lower(email), but the only query that reads by email is CustomerRepository.findByEmailIgnoreCase, which Spring Data renders as `where upper(c.email) = upper(?)`. A functional index on lower(email) cannot serve an upper() predicate, and ux_customers_email (plain email) cannot serve it either, so sign-in seq-scans customers on every attempt. That was cheap while customers held two seeded rows; this change makes the table grow without bound from an unauthenticated endpoint, so sign-in latency now grows linearly with sign-up volume, and sign-in is already the slowest endpoint in the service (an Argon2 verify runs on every attempt, including unknown accounts). The index is correct as a constraint; it is just not the index the read path needs.

findings.suggestion: Bound the hashing work rather than only metering the callers: put sign-up (and ideally sign-in) hashing behind a Semaphore or a fixed executor sized to the available cores, refusing with 429/503 past the queue rather than accumulating threads. Measure by running N concurrent sign-ups (N = 2x cores and 10x cores) while sampling redirect p99 in the same process; the number that matters is redirect latency under sign-up load, not sign-up throughput. Also record the JVM heap/container memory headroom against 200 x 16 MiB in the runbook.
findings.summary: POST /api/v1/customers puts an Argon2id hash (m=16384 KiB, t=2, ~25 ms, 16 MiB transient per call) on an unauthenticated path with no global concurrency bound. Tomcat's default 200 request threads means a worst case of ~200 concurrent hashes, i.e. ~3.2 GiB of transient allocation and full CPU saturation in the same JVM that serves the redirect path, which has no CPU isolation from it. The only defence is the per-IP SIGN_UP bucket at 60/min, which (a) does not bound aggregate concurrency across many source addresses and (b) fails open by design when Redis is unreachable (RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter line 67-ish), so the vector is fully open in exactly the degraded state where the service is least able to absorb it. The duplicate-sign-up path pays the full hash before the constraint refuses it, so a repeat flood against one known address costs the same as real sign-ups. Sign-in already has this shape, so this is a second equal entry point rather than a new class of problem — but it doubles it, and it is the one being added.

findings.suggestion: Take the cache invalidation off the open transaction — commit the insert, then invalidate before returning (the pre-issue ordering still holds relative to the response) — or at minimum set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size explicitly against expected concurrency and document the interaction. Confirm by running the existing AnonymousCreateDegradationTest variant with Redis latency injected (e.g. a proxy adding 800 ms) while watching hikaricp_connections_pending and redirect p99 on /actuator/prometheus.
findings.summary: createAnonymous holds an open database transaction across a Redis round trip: saveAndFlush inserts the row, then resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing does a network call to Redis with a 1s timeout, all inside @Transactional. The connection pool is Hikari at its default maximum of 10 (nothing in application.yml sizes it). When Redis is slow rather than down — the common failure — each create pins a pooled connection for up to ~1s in the evict alone, plus up to ~1s more in the rate-limit call before the handler is entered; ten concurrent creates exhaust the pool and the redirect path's cache-miss fallback to PostgreSQL then queues behind them. The failure is self-amplifying: a degraded Redis makes the limiter fail open, so the anonymous endpoint becomes unmetered at precisely the moment each request is holding a connection for a second. The shape is pre-existing in create(), but create() is authenticated and customer-bucketed; this replicates it on an unauthenticated, IP-bucketed path.

findings.suggestion: Replace the loop with a single `boolean existsByHostIn(Collection<String> candidates)` over the pre-computed parent chain (at most ~6 entries, bounded by label count), turning N round trips into one. Nothing about the label-based matching semantics changes.
findings.summary: isListed issues one existsByHost query per label of the host: a.b.c.example.com costs five sequential database round trips, and each create pays this before it inserts. The rows are index-hits so each is cheap, but the round trips are serialised inside the create transaction and this change puts the same loop on an unauthenticated endpoint at 30/min/IP. Creates are not the hot path, so this is latency on a low-volume route rather than a capacity problem — filed because the fix is one line and the loop is now reachable without a credential.

findings.suggestion: Make it a partial index: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_links_owner_listing_owned ON links (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL`, then drop the old one, in a follow-up migration (CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside Flyway's transaction — needs the mixed/non-transactional setting). Worth doing only once anonymous rows are a measurable fraction of the table; check with `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_id IS NULL), count(*) FROM links` and pg_relation_size on the index.
findings.summary: ix_links_owner_listing (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) will now index anonymous rows it can never serve: every owner-scoped query is an equality match on customer_id and SQL equality never matches NULL, so each anonymous link adds an index entry that no query can read. On the busiest table in the system, at a permitted 30 creates/min/IP with no reaper, that is monotonic index growth for zero read benefit — larger index, slower vacuum, more buffer cache spent on unreachable tuples. Impact is proportional to anonymous adoption, which nobody can estimate yet; at low volume it is invisible.

findings.suggestion: Prepend `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` to V4 (and to V3) so the migration fails fast and retryably rather than queueing readers behind it, and note in the deploy runbook that the retry is expected behaviour. Confirm the lock class with `SELECT mode FROM pg_locks` during a rehearsal on a copy carrying production-sized links.
findings.summary: ALTER TABLE links ALTER COLUMN customer_id DROP NOT NULL is a catalogue-only change and rewrites nothing, but it still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on links. Flyway runs it at application startup with no lock_timeout, so if any in-flight statement holds even a weak lock on links, the ALTER waits — and while it waits, every subsequent query on links queues behind it, including the redirect path's cache-miss fallback. The blast is bounded by the cache absorbing most reads for 60 seconds, but the mechanism turns a fast DDL into a stall on the hot table with no ceiling. V3's CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY) has the same shape against customers: it blocks writes on customers for the duration of the build, which is trivial today at two rows and stops being trivial once sign-up has been live a while.

findings.suggestion: Ship a metric before the endpoint gets traffic: gauge `links` row count split by customer_id IS NULL, and total relation size, on the existing Prometheus endpoint. Decide a retention policy for expired anonymous rows (archive-then-delete keeping the code reserved) if the anonymous share passes some agreed fraction of the table.
findings.summary: Anonymous links expire after 30 days but are never removed: V1 states 'nothing is ever deleted' and there is no reaper, so an anonymous row occupies the links table, the ux_links_domain_code index and the (domain, code) namespace permanently while being unredirectable after a month and undeletable by anyone (no owner, no admin endpoint). The migration comment names 'let the TTL drain' as the rollback plan, which is true of redirect behaviour but not of storage. I cannot size this from the code — it depends entirely on adoption of an endpoint that has never been exposed — so this is flagged as something to watch rather than something to fix now.

not_examined: Nothing was run: no load test, no profiler, no query plans. Every claim about index usage is read from the generated-query shape and the migration text, not from EXPLAIN output.

Hibernate's physical connection handling mode was assumed to be the Spring Boot default (delayed acquisition, release after transaction). If it acquires eagerly at transaction start, the Argon2 hash in SignUpService also runs while holding a pooled connection, which would upgrade PERF-2/PERF-3 into one worse finding.

Lettuce/Spring Data Redis retry and connection-pool behaviour under partial failure was assumed from the 1s timeout in application.yml; I did not verify whether a call can exceed that (e.g. connect plus command, or reconnection attempts).
The test sources under service/src/test were read only for what they imply about production behaviour; test runtime, container reuse and suite duration were not assessed (test-adequacy's lane).
Actual Postgres lock classes for the two DDL statements were reasoned from the statement type, not observed on a real instance.
JWT verification cost per authenticated request, the click flush job's behaviour at high link cardinality, and the abuse-report path were left alone as unchanged by this diff.

No production or staging traffic figures were available, so every 'how often does this run' answer for the two new endpoints is a guess bounded by the configured rate limits (30/min and 60/min per source address) rather than a measurement.
output.summary: The change does not touch the redirect hot path, and that is the most important thing to say: LinkResolver, ResolutionCache, RedirectController and the Redis click counter are byte-identical, the anonymous link resolves through the same (domain, code) unique index, and no per-click work is added. Nothing in this diff makes a redirect slower. The risk has moved onto the two new unauthenticated write endpoints and onto the schema. Three findings are worth a decision before ship: the new lower(email) unique index does not serve findByEmailIgnoreCase (which Spring Data renders with upper()), so sign-in seq-scans a table that this change makes grow without bound (PERF-1); sign-up puts a 16 MiB, ~25 ms memory-hard hash on an unauthenticated path with no global concurrency ceiling, defended only by a per-IP bucket that fails open when Redis is unreachable (PERF-2); and anonymous create holds a pooled connection (Hikari default 10, unsized) across a Redis call inside its transaction, which under a slow Redis is exactly when the limiter stops metering it (PERF-3). The rest is proportionate housekeeping: an N-round-trip denylist walk, an index that will carry rows it can never serve, two migrations without lock_timeout, and unbounded row growth I cannot size. At the traffic this service plausibly sees on creation endpoints — orders of magnitude below the click path — none of PERF-4 through PERF-7 will be felt for a long time; PERF-1 and PERF-2 are the ones whose cost lands on an existing endpoint (sign-in) and on shared CPU with the redirect path.

findings.suggestion: Fix the document, not the code: the 400-vs-422 split is pinned elsewhere in the contract and the blind test branch reached the same reading (Fixtures.UNPARSEABLE_OUT_OF_RANGE_NUMERIC_URL, "No host from URI: 400"). Replace the `999.999.999.999` / empty-label examples in the 422 paragraph with `4294967296`, and say explicitly that out-of-range forms URI cannot parse remain 400.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 79-82 ("Host policy and equivalent forms") and the 422 description at line 704 name `999.999.999.999` and "an empty label" as hosts that "cannot be canonicalised unambiguously" and are "refused with 422 url_rejected, never accepted and never downgraded to 400". They are in fact 400 invalid_request: java.net.URI.getHost() returns null for `http://999.999.999.999/`, `http://a..b/` and `http://1.2.3.4.5/` (verified on the same JDK 21.0.12 the pom targets), so parseOrThrow refuses them before requireShortenable/HostNormalizer ever runs. The spec contradicts itself - lines 98-101 say forms URI cannot parse a host from stay 400 - and the code follows the second sentence. Only hosts URI does parse and the normaliser then rejects (e.g. `http://4294967296/`) actually reach 422; that path works.

findings.suggestion: Either document the exception - "405 and 415 carry the framework's default body and are not part of the ApiError catalogue" - or add handlers mapping them onto ApiError (which needs a new catalogue entry, so it is a contract change). Recommend documenting, since the closed catalogue has no code that means "method not allowed".
findings.summary: openapi.yaml line 121 states "Every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape" and the catalogue is closed, but there is no handler for HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException, HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException or a generic Exception. The 405 the spec explicitly requires on the two new exempt paths (lines 58-61) therefore carries Spring's BasicErrorController body - {"timestamp":...,"status":405,"error":"Method Not Allowed","path":"/api/v1/customers"} - not ApiError. Same for 415 on a wrong Content-Type and 500 on anything unhandled. Newly consequential because 405 on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links is now reachable with no credentials at all, and the default body echoes the request path.

findings.suggestion: Add one sentence to the "Three surfaces" section recording that OPTIONS on the exempt paths answers 200 with an Allow header, or set spring.mvc.dispatch-options-request=false if the intent was 405 for every non-POST verb. Decide it rather than leave it to the default.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 57-61 say the exemption is not method-aware and that non-POST verbs on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links "must reach Spring's dispatcher and answer 405". OPTIONS is not one of the four verbs listed and, with Spring MVC's default dispatchOptionsRequest=true, an unauthenticated `OPTIONS /api/v1/customers` answers 200 with `Allow: POST,OPTIONS` rather than 405 - undocumented behaviour on a path that is outside the session filter (the same request against /api/v1/links is 401, so the two new paths behave differently). Confidence is medium because this rests on a framework default rather than on code in this diff.

findings.suggestion: Either renumber so the nullable relaxation runs first, as the contract states, or amend note 7 to record the order actually shipped and why. The human on the migration diff needs the two to agree.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml note 7 (lines 249-252) pins the order of the two schema changes: "relax links.customer_id to nullable, and add a unique index over lower(email)", in that order. The implementation ships them the other way round - V3 is the unique index, V4 is the nullable relaxation. Note 7 also warns that the lower(email) index fails to apply where duplicates exist; on the shipped order that failure aborts Flyway before customer_id is relaxed, so a partially-migrated database is one where the anonymous-create path's column constraint is still NOT NULL. The 409 account_unavailable contract depends on the V3 index existing, so the dependency itself is satisfied.

findings.suggestion: Truncate to ChronoUnit.MICROS in LinkService as SignUpService already does, so the created-response value is the value that is stored and read back.
findings.summary: Timestamp precision is inconsistent across responses for the same resource. SignUpService truncates to microseconds (SignUpService.java:57) so the body matches what the TIMESTAMP(6) column will return, but LinkService.create/createAnonymous use a raw Instant.now(), so the 201 body carries nanosecond precision (e.g. ...T12:00:00.123456789Z) while a later GET /api/v1/links/{code} returns the rounded stored value (...123457Z). Both are valid ISO-8601 instants per openapi.yaml line 152, so this is not a schema break, but createdAt/expiresAt for one link differ between the create response and every subsequent read.

not_examined: Nothing was executed: no build, no integration run, no live request. Every status above is inferred from source plus one standalone compile of HostNormalizer, so framework-default behaviours (405/415 bodies, OPTIONS handling, Jackson's ISO-8601 instant rendering) are read, not observed.
POST /api/v1/sessions: the token itself - claims, issuer, the 24-hour expiresAt value in SignInResponse, and Bearer tokenType - was not traced into JwtIssuer/JwtVerifier.

The 429 path end to end: I read RateLimitGuard, the Retry-After flooring and the bucket-to-capacity mapping, but not redis/token_bucket.lua, so the retry-millis value feeding Retry-After is unverified.

GET /api/v1/links paging: the 400 boundaries (page<0, size 1..100) were read in the controller, but the LinkPage totals, the createdAt-desc/code-asc ordering and its stability across pages were not exercised.
POST /api/v1/links/{code}/abuse-reports error paths: the 400 for a reason over 500 characters and the 429 body were not traced; only the 202 path and the anonymous-link takedown were read.
clickCount exactness (durable total plus un-flushed Redis delta) and the ClickFlushJob interaction with the value reported by GET /api/v1/links/{code}.

The seeded fixtures the contract freezes: the V1/V2 migrations, the two seeded accounts' Argon2id hashes and the threat-denylist seed rows were not opened, so "alice@example.com signs in after the lower(email) index lands" is unverified.

Undocumented surfaces the spec never mentions: the actuator endpoints exposed in application.yml (health, info, metrics, prometheus) sit outside the session filter and were not compared against the contract, since the spec declares no operations for them.
Whether a request to an exempt path with an odd encoding (trailing slash, %2e, matrix parameters) still matches the exact-equality exemption - a routing/security question I left to that lens.
output.summary: The implementation honours the contract on every documented status, body and header I was able to check by reading, including the parts most likely to drift. The three 1.1.0 additions are faithful: POST /api/v1/customers is 201 with {customerId,email,createdAt} and no Location and no token, with 409 account_unavailable decided by the lower(email) unique index rather than a read-then-write; POST /api/v1/public/links is 201 with the narrower AnonymousLinkResponse (no status, no clickCount), no Location, owner column NULL, the anonymous TTL applied server-side, and a separate CreateAnonymousLinkRequest record so that alias/expiresAt are 400 under fail-on-unknown-properties rather than silently accepted; both paths are exempted from the session filter by exact string equality, not by prefix, and both charge their own IP-keyed bucket. The click path still returns 302 (not 301) with Location verbatim plus the pinned no-store/Pragma/Expires trio on redirect, 404 and 429 alike, and the single not_found body is a shared constant so it is byte-identical everywhere. Error bodies come from one closed ErrorCode catalogue with fields omitted unless invalid_request, and Retry-After is floored at 1 second. The equivalent-form work is genuinely shared: I compiled HostNormalizer and confirmed the spec's worked cases (2130706433, 0x7f000001, 017700000001, 0177.0.0.1, 012.0.0.1, trailing dot, IPv6 mapped, five-part names) all canonicalise as documented, and both UrlValidator and DenylistThreatCheck decide on its output. The most consequential divergence is documentary rather than behavioural: the spec's own examples of a host that "cannot be canonicalised" - 999.999.999.999 and a..b - are 400, not the 422 the document twice promises, because java.net.URI extracts no host from them and the syntax gate fires first (API-1); the document contradicts itself on this and the code follows the other sentence, so I would change the document. Beyond that, the undeclared verbs the contract deliberately leaves at 405 answer with Spring's default error body rather than ApiError, contradicting "every non-2xx has the ApiError shape" (API-2), and OPTIONS on the two new unauthenticated paths answers 200 rather than 405 by framework default (API-3). Nothing here is a break a caller could be harmed by today; all five findings are decisions somebody should take explicitly rather than inherit.

findings.suggestion: Extract `private URI acceptableTarget(String longUrl)` containing the three calls and have both create and createAnonymous call it. The design's reason for two public methods (different request/response types, different expiry) is unaffected — only the shared acceptance rule moves.
findings.summary: The three-call target-acceptance sequence (parseOrThrow / requireShortenable / requirePermittedTarget) is now written twice, in create and createAnonymous. AC12 requires the two paths to accept exactly the same targets, and the javadoc on createAnonymous asserts that in prose, but nothing in the code enforces it: a fourth check added to create in six months is silently absent from the anonymous path. This is duplication of the kind that drifts, and it is the security-relevant kind.

findings.suggestion: Add `private String shortUrl(String code)` and use it from both toResponse and the AnonymousLinkResponse construction; keep the two response builders separate since the DTOs genuinely differ.
findings.summary: createAnonymous builds its response inline while every other read path in the class goes through toResponse, and `baseUrl + "/" + link.getCode()` is now spelled in two places. The short-URL join is the sort of thing that acquires trailing-slash handling later in one copy only.

findings.suggestion: Throw IllegalStateException from the constructor when a non-null ownHost does not normalise (it is bean construction, so it fails the context rather than a request), or at minimum log.warn once naming the host and stating that the self-referential check is inactive.
findings.summary: `canonicalOwnHost = HostNormalizer.normalize(ownHost).orElse(null)` silently degrades: if app.base-url's host ever fails to canonicalise, the self-referential-target rule disappears at startup with no log line and no failure, and the only symptom is short links pointing at short links. Elsewhere this codebase is careful to log the moment a protection stops applying (see the fail-open warn in LinkService.requirePermittedTarget and JwtSessionService's ephemeral-key warning).

findings.suggestion: Have valueOf take the radix as a parameter (the caller can obtain it once) and return OptionalLong, or keep the long sentinel but name it (`private static final long NOT_AN_ADDRESS_PART = -1L`) so the two failure encodings are at least both self-describing.
findings.summary: Two different sentinel conventions live within twenty lines: radixOf returns NOT_A_NUMBER (0) and valueOf returns -1, so asDottedQuad has to test `part < 0` for one failure and callers test `== NOT_A_NUMBER` for the other. valueOf also recomputes radixOf for a part isAddressCandidate has already classified, so the classification exists twice.

findings.suggestion: Either rename to SignUpController to match SignInController and its service, or leave it and accept that customer-resource endpoints belong here. Worth one line either way; the current pairing is the only inconsistency.
findings.summary: CustomerController is named for the resource while its immediate sibling SignInController is named for the action, and it delegates to SignUpService. Nothing is wrong today — one endpoint, one collaborator — but the name promises the customer resource generally, so the next customer endpoint (GET /customers/{id}, password change) will land here by name rather than by cohesion.

not_examined: service/src/test/** — the test diff (~2,400 lines) is the test-adequacy reviewer's brief; I read it only where it clarified production intent
artifacts/openapi.yaml and the DTOs under api/ — frozen contract files owned by the API-contract lens
Correctness of the IPv4/IDN canonicalisation itself, and of the V3/V4 migrations against a real database — out of this lens's brief
Performance of the added query and hashing paths
output.summary: Clean change overall, and unusually well documented: the comments say why (NULL owner vs sentinel row in V4, hand-rolled IPv4 parsing, no Location header, the pre-apply duplicate check on V3) rather than what, and they match the house style of the surrounding code. Structure is right — business rules in SignUpService and LinkService, controllers only rate-limit and delegate; rate-limiting goes through the existing RateLimitGuard in the existing shape; log lines match SignInService's identity-free convention; no swallowed exceptions (the two catches translate a constraint violation and a dependency failure, both commented). The findings worth acting on are CLEAN-1 (the acceptance sequence duplicated between the owned and anonymous create paths, where AC12 requires them to agree and only prose enforces it) and CLEAN-3 (a security check that can silently switch itself off at startup). The remaining three are taste; the rest of the diff's minor points were consistent with the code around them and are not filed.

findings.suggestion: Decide explicitly whether an account of age zero may take a link down. Cheapest closures that need no new subsystem: (a) require the reporter's account to pre-date the reported link, or to be older than some app.abuse.min-reporter-age; (b) queue rather than block when the reporter has no links of their own, so the immediate-takedown power stays with established accounts; or (c) add a second bucket keyed by client address alongside the customer-id bucket, so minting accounts does not multiply takedown capacity. Whichever is chosen, add a test to SignUpIsolationTest asserting the outcome of a fresh account reporting another customer's code - that assertion is currently absent and is the security control this finding is about.
findings.summary: Self-service sign-up silently re-scopes every authenticated endpoint from "two hand-provisioned accounts" to "anyone on the internet", and the one authenticated capability that deliberately crosses tenant boundaries is the abuse-report takedown. report() resolves by (domain, code) with no owner scoping and immediately markBlocked()s the link, with no moderation queue and no unblock path (both explicitly out of scope). The only defence is ABUSE_REPORT keyed by customer id at 60/min - and after this change an attacker mints customer ids at 60/min per IP through POST /api/v1/customers, so the per-reporter bucket bounds nothing. Any published short link (and short links are published by definition) can now be permanently killed by an unauthenticated stranger who spends one sign-up. impact.json recorded this data flow as risk "low" on the stated basis that "only signed-in callers can report", which AC4 makes vacuous; SignUpIsolationTest pins that a new account cannot read/modify/delete/list another customer's link but does not pin what it can do to one via abuse-reports.

findings.suggestion: Make the fail-open decision per bucket rather than global: keep ALLOWED-on-error for CLICK and NOT_FOUND (a 429'd redirect is a self-inflicted outage), and fail closed with 503 service_unavailable for SIGN_UP. That is the same shape AC15 already asks for - degradation spent on refusing new writes, never on serving clicks - and it makes the sign-up path behave under a Redis outage the way the anonymous-create path already does. A boolean on RateLimitBucket, or a set of buckets consulted in the catch at line 67, is enough.
findings.summary: The limiter fails open on an unreachable Redis (deliberate, pre-existing, and correct for the click path). Anonymous link creation is incidentally protected from that during a Redis outage because ResolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing throws 503 before a row is written. POST /api/v1/customers has no such gate: it touches only PostgreSQL, so with Redis down it is completely unmetered - unbounded 16 MiB/~25 ms Argon2id hashes (Tomcat's 200 default threads x 16 MiB is ~3.2 GiB of native memory), unbounded customer rows, and unbounded account minting, which compounds SEC-1 exactly when the operator is already busy. The requirement's non-functional list says an unauthenticated endpoint that writes to the database must not become an unmetered storage-burn vector; today the only thing enforcing that on sign-up is a dependency the design documents as fail-open.

findings.suggestion: Hash before the transaction opens: compute the encoded hash in the controller or in a non-transactional method and pass it into a small @Transactional insert, so the connection is held only for the saveAndFlush. Behaviour, including the 409-from-constraint semantics, is unchanged.
findings.summary: passwordHasher.hash() runs inside the @Transactional signUp method, so each unauthenticated sign-up holds a pooled JDBC connection for the ~25 ms of memory-hard Argon2id work before it does any SQL. At the configured 60/min per IP (and unbounded per SEC-2) this starves the HikariCP pool, and the pool is shared with the click path's PostgreSQL fallback on a resolution-cache miss - the one path the requirement says degradation must never be spent on. SignInService has the same shape, so this is a pattern rather than a novelty, but sign-up doubles the exposed surface and adds a write.

findings.suggestion: The design's rejection of DNS is defensible on TOCTOU grounds and I would not overturn it here. But record the residual gap where an operator will see it, and consider the cheap partial: refuse hosts whose canonical form ends in a label set known to be a loopback-mapping wildcard, or resolve at create time as a defence-in-depth signal that is allowed to fail open on lookup error. What would raise my confidence that this is acceptable rather than an oversight is a line in artifacts/design.json or docs/OPERATIONS.md stating that name-to-internal-address targets are knowingly out of scope.
findings.summary: HostNormalizer closes textual and numeric equivalence well (I checked the trailing-dot, case, IDN, empty-label, hex/octal/short-form and out-of-range paths against java.net.URI's own host parsing and they hold, including the InetAddress.getByName("0177.0.0.1") trap the design calls out). But isInternal() returns false for anything that is not an IP literal and no DNS is resolved, so the simplest equivalent form of an internal address - a registered name that resolves to one - is still accepted: http://127.0.0.1.nip.io/, http://localtest.me/, or any attacker-controlled A record pointing at 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254. The requirement's non-functional line asks the filter to resist equivalent-form evasion generally rather than only the two confirmed forms. Impact is bounded because nothing in this service fetches the target server-side (I grepped: no RestTemplate/WebClient/HttpClient/URLConnection anywhere in main), so this is not SSRF against us - the exposure is the clicker's own network, e.g. a corporate browser reaching an internal console via one of our links.

findings.suggestion: Either write the deployment precondition into docs/OPERATIONS.md (the proxy must preserve the source address, e.g. PROXY protocol, or these limits are global ceilings and 30/min will be hit by ordinary traffic), or add a configurable trusted-proxy list so X-Forwarded-For can be honoured only from known hops. Note application.yml is a protected path, so a config-side fix needs a human either way.
findings.summary: Both new unauthenticated buckets key on httpRequest.getRemoteAddr() and deliberately do not trust X-Forwarded-For (a sound default with no trusted-proxy list). The requirement states the service sits behind an edge proxy. If that proxy terminates the connection without a PROXY-protocol or trusted-header path, getRemoteAddr() is the proxy for every request, so ANONYMOUS_CREATE (30/min) and SIGN_UP (60/min) become service-wide ceilings: one caller can consume the entire anonymous-create budget and deny the new feature to everybody, and neither bucket provides any per-attacker protection - which is the whole of what AC14 asks it for. The design explicitly deferred this to the runbook; docs/OPERATIONS.md was edited in this change and does not mention it, so the stated mitigation does not exist.

findings.suggestion: Log the client address on the anonymous create path (it is already in hand at PublicLinkController line 54 and is the key the bucket is charged against), or pass it into createAnonymous for the log line only. This is deliberately not a proposal to store it on the row - a log line gives incident response a handle without adding a personal-data column to links.
findings.summary: An anonymously created link records no attribution at all: customer_id is NULL by design, and the log line is "Created anonymous link {code}" with no client address. When one of these links turns out to be a phishing redirect there is nothing to trace it to and no way to find the creator's other links, so the only response available is per-code abuse reports - which is the one takedown route that requires an account (SEC-1) and which nobody can use without already holding the code. The requirement asks that new behaviour be observable through the existing logging surface.

findings.suggestion: If the oracle is accepted, tighten signUpPerMinute well below the sign-in bucket (they defend different things: sign-in throttles guesses at one known account, sign-up throttles enumeration of all of them) and close SEC-2 so the bound cannot evaporate. If it is not accepted, that is a contract change and belongs with whoever ratifies artifacts/openapi.yaml, not with implement.
findings.summary: 409 account_unavailable is an account-existence oracle on an unauthenticated endpoint, in a service that goes to real lengths elsewhere to avoid being one (identical 401s, timing-equalised sign-in, no 403, no 410). The design node states this plainly and asks a reviewer to accept or reject it, so I am recording it from the review side rather than re-arguing it: AC6 does require a visible refusal and there is no wording of one that is not a disclosure. What I would push back on is the claim that the bucket makes it bounded - 60/min per IP is ~86,000 probes per address per day, and per SEC-2 it is unbounded whenever Redis is unreachable.

findings.suggestion: Reject or strip control characters from {code} before it is logged or stored - the alias/code alphabet is base62, so a single guard in the controller (or an AliasPolicy-style character check) both closes this and costs nothing. Alternatively configure a log encoder that escapes newlines.
findings.summary: The {code} path variable is percent-decoded by Spring before it reaches this log line, so POST /api/v1/links/%0aWHATEVER/abuse-reports forges an arbitrary extra line into the application log and still answers 202 (the endpoint accepts any well-formed code by design, so nothing rejects it first). RedirectController line 88 has the same shape in its catch block. This is pre-existing code that this change did not touch - I am reporting it because open sign-up moves it from "reachable by two provisioned accounts" to "reachable by anyone", which is the trust-boundary shift SEC-1 is about.

findings.suggestion: Confidence is low because the edge proxy very likely caps body size already (nginx client_max_body_size defaults to 1 MB) - confirming that cap and recording it in docs/OPERATIONS.md as a deployment precondition would close this finding without code. If the cap cannot be relied on, a small OncePerRequestFilter rejecting Content-Length above a few KB on these two paths is the in-service equivalent.
findings.summary: @Size(max = 2048) on longUrl (and @Size(max = 256) on SignUpRequest.password) is bean validation, which runs after Jackson has already materialised the whole string. Spring Boot applies no default size limit to a non-multipart, non-form request body, so an unauthenticated POST of a multi-hundred-megabyte JSON document to /api/v1/public/links or /api/v1/customers is fully parsed into heap before any constraint fires. Two new unauthenticated body-accepting endpoints widen a surface that previously existed only at POST /api/v1/sessions.

findings.suggestion: Fail fast at bean construction instead: if ownHost is non-null and does not normalise, throw from the UrlValidator constructor so a misconfigured base-url stops startup rather than quietly turning off a check nobody will notice is off.
findings.summary: canonicalOwnHost = HostNormalizer.normalize(ownHost).orElse(null) silently disables the self-referential check when the configured own host cannot be canonicalised, and line 130 then skips it because canonicalOwnHost is null. That is a fail-open inside a class whose documented contract two lines earlier is that an un-canonicalisable host fails closed. Reachable only through a misconfigured app.base-url, and the loopback rules would still catch the default localhost, so the practical exposure is small - a short link pointing at our own origin, i.e. a redirect loop through us.

not_examined: Third-party dependency vulnerabilities: service/pom.xml is byte-identical per artifacts/design.json and I did not run or inspect an SCA/CVE scan against jjwt, Spring Boot 3.5, the Argon2 provider or the Redis client.

The redis/token_bucket.lua script itself - I read its Java call site and the key namespacing (ratelimit:<bucket>:<key>, which does make AC14's no-cross-spending property mechanical) but did not read the Lua for atomicity or refill-arithmetic bugs.

Live behaviour: I ran no tests and started no service. Every claim about java.net.URI host parsing, Spring path-variable decoding and JDK numeric-literal handling is read from source and from the JDK's documented parser behaviour, not measured. The HostNormalizer worked table in particular is asserted by HostCanonicalisationTest, which I read but did not execute.

Argon2PasswordHasher parameter adequacy and the Ed25519/jjwt verification path beyond confirming verifyWith(publicKey) plus requireIssuer (which does exclude alg=none and symmetric-key confusion) - both are unchanged by this run.

The two seeded credentials in V2 and the ephemeral-session-key default when app.session.*-key-pem is blank: unchanged pre-existing configuration risks, flagged in the existing docs, deliberately left alone.

orchestrator/sdlc/gates.py and orchestrator/tests/test_gates.py appear in the diff range but carry no Run-Id trailer - they are human commits outside this run, and I did not review the gate logic or whether it can be weakened.
TLS, CORS, security response headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, referrer policy on the redirect) - all edge-proxy concerns with no representation in this repository, so I could not assess them.

Timing-side-channel measurement: I read the sign-in equalisation and believe the argument, but did not measure whether the new sign-up path leaks account existence by timing in addition to by status code.
PostgreSQL and Redis deployment configuration in docker-compose.yml - not read, so default credentials or exposed ports there are unassessed.

Whether anonymous link rows are ever reclaimed. V1 states nothing is ever deleted and I found no sweeper, so the links table grows monotonically with expired anonymous rows; I did not chase whether an external retention job exists, and treated it as capacity rather than security.
output.summary: The headline change - HostNormalizer - is the strongest part of this diff and I could not break it. I traced every documented spelling against java.net.URI's own host parser: the trailing-dot, mixed-case, IDN, empty-label, five-part-name, hex/octal/short-form and out-of-range cases all behave as specified, the label walk in DenylistThreatCheck cannot collapse a public host onto a denylisted parent, both call sites fail closed on Optional.empty(), and the decision to hand-parse numeric IPv4 rather than trust InetAddress.getByName is correct and correctly reasoned. Scheme is restricted to http/https at parseOrThrow, so javascript:/data:/file: never reach a Location header; nothing in main fetches a target server-side, so there is no SSRF sink; codes are 128 bits of CSPRNG; owner scoping is in the query rather than in a post-fetch comparison, so anonymous links are invisible by construction rather than by remembering to filter; the 405-not-401 consequence of the non-method-aware filter exemption is tested. The weakest area is not the filter at all - it is the trust boundary. AC4 turned every authenticated endpoint from "two hand-provisioned accounts" into "anyone with an HTTP client", and the one authenticated capability that deliberately crosses tenant lines is the immediate, unmoderated, irreversible abuse-report takedown, whose only limit is keyed by a customer id an attacker can now mint at will (SEC-1). Second weakest is that sign-up is the only unauthenticated write with no Redis dependency, so it is the one endpoint the fail-open limiter genuinely leaves unmetered during an outage (SEC-2), which compounds the first. The remainder are smaller: a name-resolves-to-loopback gap the design knowingly left open (SEC-4), a rate-limit keying precondition the design consigned to a runbook that was edited in this change and does not carry it (SEC-5), no attribution for anonymous creates (SEC-6), and the account-existence oracle the design node explicitly asked a reviewer to adjudicate (SEC-7).

findings.suggestion: On a scratch worktree, revert only implement's three normalisation hunks — HostNormalizer's body, UrlValidator.requireShortenable (line 129-131), DenylistThreatCheck.evaluate (line 55-64) — and run HostEvasionRefusalTest and HostCanonicalisationTest against the current test tree. Attach the failing output (expect aDenylistedHostWithATrailingDotIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheHostItself and anInternalAddressWrittenAsOneDecimalNumberIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheDottedForm red) to the run record as AC3's evidence, or have a human waive the ordering constraint explicitly.
findings.summary: AC3 has two halves and only one is evidenced. The tests exist and are retained, but "fail against the pre-change code" was never observed: the run journal shows `author-tests` and `implement` started in parallel (seq 71-72), author-tests' exit gates were tests_compile / tests_not_weakened / paths_confined with no execution, and the first suite run was `maven_verify` at the `verify` node, after the join — i.e. only ever against the fixed code. plan.json's T1 names "run log entry recording the failing run against pre-change code" as a deliverable and there is no such entry; test-contract.json's own rationale flagged this as "a pipeline obligation... the single easiest thing here to lose". By inspection the test does discriminate (pre-change, requireShortenable lower-cased the raw host and DenylistThreatCheck matched the raw host, so https://malware.example.com./x returned 201), but "by inspection" is exactly what AC3 refuses. Release-readiness must not mark AC3 met on the strength of a green post-fix suite.

findings.suggestion: Add a behaviour whose only outcome is the refusal — e.g. anonymousCreateIsRefusedWith503WhenTheCacheCannotBeInvalidated — asserting exactly 503, error=service_unavailable and message "Temporarily unable to accept new links." with the counter tier paused, rather than tolerating the success. If a 201 genuinely remains permissible for the shared tier, drive the outage at the dependency the pre-issue invalidation actually needs so one answer is determined.
findings.summary: The behaviour named for AC15 cannot fail on the thing AC15 asks for. anonymousCreationIsRefusedWithTheExistingErrorWhileADependencyIsUnavailable accepts `201 || 503`, and its three following assertions on the service_unavailable envelope are filtered on `statusCode() != 201` / `== 503`, so they are all vacuous when the answer is 201. Delete `resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(...)` from LinkService.createAnonymous — the one call that produces the 503 there — and this test still passes. The guarantee survives only through bothCreatePathsDegradeTheSameWay, which compares the two paths' statuses; that single equality is the whole pin, and the same disjunctive tolerance on the authenticated path was already recorded as a finding in the previous run's review-test-adequacy.json.

findings.suggestion: A unit test in com.example.urlshortener.unit — UrlValidator is deliberately constructible without Spring (LinkPolicyConfig's javadoc says so) — e.g. ownHostIsRefusedInEverySpelling: `new UrlValidator("short.example")` and assert url_rejected for https://short.example./x and https://SHORT.Example/x, and no exception for https://notshort.example/x. Optionally the HTTP counterpart with app.base-url=https://short.example overridden on its own context.
findings.summary: New behaviour with no test that can see it: the self-referential check now compares canonical hosts (canonicalOwnHost, computed once in the constructor) so that a trailing-dot or numeric spelling of the shortener's own host is refused. No test distinguishes it. app.base-url is http://localhost:8080 in every context the suite boots, so ownHost is "localhost", and isInternal("localhost") returns true regardless — every spelling of the own host is refused by the internal-address rule whether or not canonicalisation happens. Revert line 130 to the previous `host.equals(ownHost.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))` and the suite stays green; Fixtures.SELF_REFERENTIAL_URL (http://localhost:8080/somewhere) does not separate the two rules either.

findings.suggestion: Give this class a longer override (e.g. app.links.anonymous-ttl=PT10S) so the mid-life click has seconds of margin rather than a fraction of one, or assert the 302 only after re-reading the clock on the response and failing with a message that names the elapsed time. Do not relax the 302 expectation itself.
findings.summary: Timing slack too thin for the click path this suite runs. The class configures a 3-second anonymous TTL and anAnonymousLinkRedirectsUntilItsExpiryPasses sleeps half of it, then requires a click to return 302. The guard `halfWay.isBefore(link.expiresAt())` is read before the request is sent, so a click that straddles the expiry passes the guard and fails on the 302 — and a served redirect makes up to three sequential Redis round trips each carrying the configured 1s command timeout, against ~1.4s of remaining margin. This is the one behaviour pinning "live for the whole period it was promised" (AC10); if it flakes it gets muted and takes that claim with it.

findings.suggestion: Annotate the method @ResourceLock(Resources.LOCALE) so JUnit serialises it if parallel execution is ever enabled, and leave the assertion as it is.
findings.summary: caseIsNotPartOfAHost mutates JVM-global state (Locale.setDefault("tr")) to prove the lower-casing is locale-independent. It is restored in a finally and there is no junit-platform.properties enabling parallelism, so it is safe today — but it is a shared-JVM global in a suite that boots Spring contexts, and the day parallel execution is turned on this becomes order-dependent flakiness in whatever else happens to format a string. The behaviour is worth pinning; the hazard is worth declaring.

findings.suggestion: If it is worth keeping, pin it where it is observable: a unit test calling DenylistThreatCheck.evaluate directly with URI.create("http://4294967296/") and asserting ThreatVerdict.BLOCK, independent of the validator having run first.
findings.summary: The fail-closed branch added here (canonical.isEmpty() -> BLOCK) is unreachable through any endpoint: UrlValidator.requireShortenable already throws url_rejected on an un-canonicalisable host before the threat check runs, so no test would notice if this branch were deleted. Its own comment states the point — "a security property that holds only because they run in a particular order is one reordering away from not holding" — and that property, independence from ordering, is precisely what no test asserts. Defence in depth deliberately added, recorded so it is a decision rather than dead code somebody later prunes.

not_examined: The 132 pre-existing test methods: I read DegradedDependencyTest in full (to judge whether AnonymousCreateDegradationTest's 201-or-503 tolerance matched an existing convention) and grepped the rest. AC17's "the existing test suite passes unchanged" I took from the verify node's maven_verify gate, not by reading those tests.
I did not run the suite. Every claim about flakiness, timing margin or a test passing after a hypothetical revert is from reading the code, not from execution or repeated runs.

findings.suggestion: Hash outside the transaction: make signUp() non-transactional, compute the hash, then call a small @Transactional insert method (separate bean, so the proxy applies). Alternatively set spring.datasource.hikari.auto-commit=false with spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true so acquisition is genuinely lazy — but that is a protected-path config edit and does not remove the CPU cost from the request. Either way, size the pool explicitly. Confirm before/after by counting rows in pg_stat_activity with state='idle in transaction' during a sign-up burst, and by HikariCP's connection-acquisition timer.
findings.summary: signUp() is @Transactional and computes the Argon2id hash (m=16384 KiB, t=2, ~25 ms) as the first thing inside the transaction, before any statement is issued. With Hikari's default autoCommit=true, Hibernate acquires the JDBC connection at transaction begin (to turn autocommit off) rather than at first statement, so a pool connection sits idle-in-transaction for the whole hash. application.yml sets no spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size, so the pool is the default 10 and is shared with the redirect cache-miss path. At 60 sign-ups/min/IP the aggregate is bounded only by the number of source addresses: ~400 sign-ups/s in flight would hold all 10 connections, and the endpoint that starves is the click path's PostgreSQL fallback.

findings.suggestion: Bound concurrent hashing rather than the per-IP rate: wrap PasswordHasher.hash/matches in a Semaphore sized to something like the core count (queue or 503 beyond it), or cap server.tomcat.threads.max so the worst case is arithmetic somebody has checked. Confirm with a heap/allocation profile under a concurrent sign-up burst and by asserting the deployed -Xmx against threads × 16 MiB.
findings.summary: Nothing bounds the number of concurrent Argon2id hashes. Each one allocates 16 MiB; Tomcat's default max-threads is 200 and no thread cap or heap size is configured in this repository, so 200 concurrent sign-ups is ~3.2 GiB of transient allocation plus 200 threads of memory-hard CPU. The per-IP SIGN_UP bucket (60/min) bounds one caller, not aggregate concurrency, and the limiter fails open when Redis is unreachable (RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter, allow-on-exception), so during a Redis outage this endpoint is unmetered. Sign-in already carried this exposure and it predates the change; sign-up adds a second entry point on the same key with the same bucket, roughly doubling it.

findings.suggestion: Put `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` at the top of the migration so it fails fast and is retried rather than head-of-line blocking reads, and run it in a low-traffic window. Confirm by checking pg_locks for the granted/waiting chain on links while it applies in staging.
findings.summary: ALTER TABLE links ALTER COLUMN customer_id DROP NOT NULL is catalog-only and instant, but it needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on links — the table the redirect path reads on every cache miss. With no lock_timeout set, the ALTER queues behind any in-flight query on links and, while it waits, every later query on links queues behind it. On a busy instance that turns a millisecond of DDL into a stall of the hot path for as long as the longest running query, during a deploy, with Flyway blocking startup behind it.

findings.suggestion: Make it partial: CREATE INDEX ... ON links (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL, as a separate migration once anonymous volume is known. Confirm with pg_relation_size on the index and a count of NULL-owner rows after a few weeks.
findings.summary: ix_links_owner_listing (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) now carries anonymous rows for the first time: a btree indexes NULLs, and every anonymous link adds an entry under a leading NULL that no query can ever match, because findOwnedBy and findByDomainAndCodeAndCustomerId are equality-scoped. The migration comment says the index 'never serves an anonymous row', which is true of reads and not of writes — the insert cost, index size and vacuum work are all paid. Magnitude depends entirely on anonymous volume, which nobody has measured; at low volume this is invisible.

findings.suggestion: Either accept it and instrument it (alert on the count of rows WHERE customer_id IS NULL and on the ANONYMOUS_CREATE 429 rate), or add a reaper that hard-deletes anonymous rows some margin past expires_at — noting that reissuing their codes is explicitly forbidden, so a reaper needs a tombstone. Decide before ship rather than after the table is large.
findings.summary: Anonymous rows accumulate without bound and nothing removes them. Expiry is derived at read time and nothing sweeps, so an expired anonymous link keeps its row, its index entries and its (domain, code) namespace slot forever, and no owner exists who could delete it. The only ceiling is the ANONYMOUS_CREATE bucket at 30/min per source address — which is per-IP, not global, and fails open when Redis is unreachable. I cannot say from the code how fast the table will grow; the honest statement is that the growth rate is set by attacker choice rather than by anything in this service.

findings.suggestion: Move invalidateBeforeIssuing outside the transactional boundary (commit the row, then invalidate, then respond — the 503-on-failure semantics can be preserved by doing it in the controller or a wrapper bean), or explicitly size the pool for the slow-Redis case. Confirm by holding Redis at a 1s delay and watching HikariCP pending-connection count.
findings.summary: createAnonymous holds the database transaction open across a Redis round trip: resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(code) runs inside @Transactional, after saveAndFlush. Redis timeouts are 1s connect and 1s read, so a Redis brownout parks a pool connection for up to ~2s per request. With the default pool of 10 and an unauthenticated caller supplying the traffic, a slow (not dead) Redis converts into connection-pool exhaustion for everything else, including the redirect cache-miss path. This mirrors the existing create() exactly — the pattern is pre-existing — but it is newly reachable without a credential.

findings.suggestion: If it is ever worth touching: build the candidate list and ask once (existsByHostIn(candidates)), and skip the parent walk entirely when the canonical host is a dotted quad.
findings.summary: isListed issues one existsByHost query per parent label, inside the create transaction — four to six round trips for an ordinary hostname. Newly, HostNormalizer canonicalises numeric hosts to dotted quads, so an IP target now walks 127.0.0.1 -> 0.0.1 -> 0.1 -> 1: four queries whose answers cannot be meaningful, on both create paths. Each is a unique-index hit on a tiny table, so the cost is round trips, not work; create is not the hot path and this is a rounding error at any load this service will plausibly see.

findings.suggestion: Note the expected build time against the production row count in the approval for this protected-path migration. If customers is ever large, split it out as a non-transactional Flyway migration using CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
findings.summary: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY, and Flyway wraps the migration in a transaction so CONCURRENTLY is not available without configuring it) takes a SHARE lock on customers for the duration of the build, blocking writes — i.e. sign-ups and nothing else, since sign-in only reads. Harmless at the current table size; worth knowing it scales with the customer count, which self-service sign-up is the thing that makes grow.

findings.suggestion: Implement Persistable<UUID> with a transient isNew flag on the entities, or inject EntityManager and call persist() directly. Confirm with hibernate SQL logging on a single sign-up: two statements today, one after.
findings.summary: CustomerEntity has an application-assigned UUID id, no @Version and does not implement Persistable, so Spring Data's isNew() sees a non-null id and routes saveAndFlush through merge() — Hibernate issues a SELECT by primary key before the INSERT. One wasted round trip per sign-up. The same is true of every link insert, so this is a pre-existing house pattern rather than something this change introduced.

not_examined: The redirect hot path itself (RedirectController, LinkResolver, ResolutionCache, RedisClickCounter, ClickFlushJob) — read to confirm it is untouched by this change, but not reviewed as new work; the impact analysis's claim that anonymous links traverse it identically checks out (CachedLink carries no customerId).

Hibernate's actual connection-acquisition timing. PERF-1 assumes eager acquisition at transaction begin, which is the behaviour with Hikari autoCommit=true and no provider_disables_autocommit; I did not verify it by running the service with DEBUG on the pool.
redis/token_bucket.lua — the limiter's Redis-side cost and key expiry were not read.
Query plans. No EXPLAIN was run against any statement; index coverage was read off the migrations only.
Deployment resource limits. There is no Dockerfile, k8s manifest or JVM flag anywhere in this repository, so heap size, CPU allocation and replica count in PERF-2 are unknown rather than assumed.

Real traffic volumes and mix. Nothing here says how many redirects, creates or sign-ups per second to expect, so every 'at what load' statement in the findings is arithmetic from configured limits, not from measurement.
Test-suite runtime and the Testcontainers changes in AbstractIntegrationTest/AbstractRestartIntegrationTest — CI cost, not service performance.
Allocation behaviour of IDN.toASCII and the split-based label walk in HostNormalizer; judged trivially small on a non-hot path and not profiled.
output.summary: The redirect path — the one that matters — is untouched: no new work, no extra round trip, no analytics write added to it, and the (domain, code) unique index still backs the only lookup it makes. Anonymous links flow through it identically. Nothing in this change makes a click slower. What the change does add is two unauthenticated write endpoints in front of a database pool that has never been sized (Hikari default 10) and a memory-hard hash with no concurrency bound. The three findings worth a human are: sign-up holds a pool connection idle through ~25 ms of Argon2 (PERF-1); nothing caps concurrent Argon2 at 16 MiB apiece against a 200-thread connector (PERF-2); and V4's ALTER TABLE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on links, the table the click path falls back to, with no lock_timeout (PERF-3). The rest is smaller: an index that now stores rows it can never serve, anonymous rows that accumulate with no reaper, a transaction held across a Redis call on the new path. None of it is measured — nobody has run this under load — so severities reflect the cost when it goes wrong and confidence reflects how much the code alone can prove.

findings.suggestion: Extract `private URI admittedTarget(String longUrl)` performing the parse, requireShortenable and requirePermittedTarget, and call it from both create() and createAnonymous(). The methods stay separate (which the design justifies); only the rule set is shared.
findings.summary: createAnonymous re-types the three-line target-admission sequence from create() (parseOrThrow, requireShortenable, requirePermittedTarget). The javadoc promises the two paths must never differ in what they accept (AC12), but nothing mechanical holds them together: a fourth rule added to create() will silently not apply to the anonymous path.

findings.suggestion: Add `private String shortUrl(LinkEntity link)` and use it from both response builders.
findings.summary: The short URL is now assembled as `baseUrl + "/" + link.getCode()` in two places (toResponse and createAnonymous). Small, but it is the kind of duplication that drifts the day baseUrl gains a trailing-slash rule or a path prefix.

findings.suggestion: Have radixOf return the digit offset alongside the radix (a small private record, or a single `parsePart` returning the value / -1), so the prefix rule exists in exactly one place.
findings.summary: The radix rules are encoded twice: radixOf decides base from the 0x/leading-zero prefix, and valueOf re-derives both the radix and the prefix length in a switch. Two encodings of the same rule in one file, and the second only makes sense if you have read the first.

findings.suggestion: Log the client address (already available to the controller for the rate-limit key) or the MDC request id with this line.
findings.summary: The duplicate-sign-up refusal logs no correlator at all - no client address, no request id - so a spike of 409s cannot be attributed to one caller versus many without a debugger. The email is rightly absent; something joinable is not.
